title: Snyder v. Phelps (district voir-dire/posttrial stage)
lead: In the district court’s posttrial ruling, the judge upheld the jury-selection process and tort verdict arising from a funeral protest, but cut punitive damages; later appellate reversal was a separate stage.

actors.name: Albert Snyder
actors.role: Father of the deceased Marine and tort plaintiff

actors.name: Fred Phelps, Shirley Phelps-Roper, Rebekah Phelps-Davis, and Westboro Baptist Church
actors.role: Defendants associated with the protest and publication

proceedings: Pretrial dismissal of two claims; jury verdict on three remaining torts; district court denied liability and new-trial challenges, kept $2.9 million compensation, and reduced punishment to $2.1 million; later appellate reversal and Supreme Court affirmance are separate reported context.
limits: This is the February 4, 2008 district ruling, not the final First Amendment disposition of the litigation. Later history is supplied by the assignment without a full separate-opinion account here. Original order confirms Fred Phelps’s punitive amount was $300,000.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A military funeral became the setting for a religious protest
sections.cue: Introduce the family and distinguish what Albert saw when.
paragraphs: Marine Lance Corporal Matthew Snyder died in Iraq on March 3, 2006. His funeral took place March 10 at a Catholic church in Westminster, Maryland. Fred Phelps, relatives, and their Westboro Baptist Church used military funerals to publicize religious views condemning American tolerance of homosexuality. They attended despite never having met Matthew or his family.

They complied with police directions and local distance rules. Albert Snyder, Matthew’s father, did not read the sign text during the procession; he later saw it on television. Shirley Phelps-Roper subsequently posted an online account accusing Matthew’s parents of raising him against God. Albert encountered it through a Google search about his son.

Albert described distress, vomiting, and difficulty separating his memories from the protest. Medical testimony addressed aggravated depression and diabetes while acknowledging difficulty separating those effects from grief and preexisting conditions. The district court distinguished general-view signs from messages it considered potentially directed at the family.

sections.title: Three tort claims reached a heavily screened jury
sections.cue: Follow pleadings, publicity precautions, and the verdict.
paragraphs: Albert sued the church and Fred Phelps in June 2006, adding Shirley Phelps-Roper and Rebekah Phelps-Davis in February 2007. Diversity supplied jurisdiction. Before trial, Judge Richard D. Bennett granted defendants summary judgment on defamation and publicity of private life: the online statements were religious opinion rather than the required defamatory communication, and the personal information was public. Intentional infliction of emotional distress, intrusion on seclusion, and civil conspiracy remained.

At the parties’ request, questionnaires went to several hundred prospective jurors concerning the protests, military, First Amendment, and screening subjects. The venire exceeded one hundred, more than triple the usual civil pool. Parties received answers before trial, and biased respondents could be excused. Everyone acknowledging prior case knowledge was individually questioned at the bench; many with fixed opinions were removed. Most prospective jurors reached the bench at some point, and lawyers questioned nearly all individually.

On October 31, 2007, the jury found for Albert on all remaining claims and awarded $2.9 million compensation. After further instructions and argument, it added $8 million punitive damages: $1.5 million per defendant for intrusion and $500,000 each for emotional distress. Defendants sought judgment as a matter of law, reconsideration, a new trial, reduction, relief from judgment, and stays.

sections.title: Bennett found the voir dire and trial management adequate
sections.cue: Identify the procedural objections the assigned passage illustrates.
paragraphs: Defendants demanded individualized questioning of every prospective juror in their preferred format. Applying Rule 47(a)’s broad trial-court discretion and focus on impartiality, Bennett found the questionnaire and extensive individual follow-up adequate to expose publicity bias. The process did not establish an unrestricted right to use any requested format.

The two self-represented defendants, Shirley and Rebekah, also alleged hostility through religious comments and interruptions. Bennett explained that the challenged comments occurred outside the jury’s presence and arose from trial evidence, without the deep antagonism required by judicial-bias precedent. Keeping an eight-to-ten-day trial moving was ordinary administration. He rejected reconsideration and related mistrial objections.

sections.title: The district judge rejected the constitutional defense and preserved liability
sections.cue: Attribute these reasons to the district stage later reversed.
paragraphs: Bennett rejected an absolute First Amendment defense. He treated Albert and the funeral as private and declined to turn an obituary into voluntary entry into public controversy. Defendants could not create publicity and then use it to alter family status. He distinguished general views from signs and online statements a jury could read as targeting the family, and rejected religious belief as automatic immunity from generally applicable tort responsibility.

Under Maryland law, he found adequate support for outrageous conduct and severe emotional injury, intrusion during bereavement, and agreement supporting conspiracy. Conspiracy required one of the underlying torts. He considered both funeral conduct and the online account despite differences in who published it.

For the separate new-trial motion, Bennett could weigh evidence and credibility rather than apply only the judgment-as-a-matter-of-law standard. He found no result against the clear weight or miscarriage of justice; false evidence was not alleged. Defendants themselves had put their religious beliefs into issue as a defense, rather than plaintiff’s counsel improperly injecting religion to inflame the jury. These were his district-court reasons, not the eventual Supreme Court’s resolution.

sections.title: Compensatory support and punitive limits required different analyses
sections.cue: Explain why compensation stayed but punishment changed.
paragraphs: Following Gasperini, the Supreme Court precedent governing federal review of state-law excessiveness, Bennett used Maryland substantive standards within federal motion procedure. He declined the state noneconomic cap because controlling intermediate appellate law excluded intentional torts, rejected certification and requests to disregard that decision, and found $2.9 million supported by testimony and medical proof.

For punitive damages, he applied constitutional guideposts and state considerations. Conduct was reprehensible, but physical injury was comparatively limited and no proof showed more publications about this family. He did not deem the punitive-to-compensatory ratio itself unconstitutional. A funeral-picketing criminal law adopted after this funeral did not automatically set the award. He distinguished Philip Morris’s concern about punishment for past harm to nonparties from counsel’s argument for deterring future conduct.

He then considered finances, relative involvement, and partial overlap between tort awards. Punitive damages became $1 million against the church, $600,000 against Shirley, $300,000 against Fred, and $200,000 against Rebekah. Compensation remained joint and several. Because reduction rested on constitutional as well as state grounds, he did not give Albert the new-trial option associated with ordinary discretionary remittitur.

sections.title: The revised district judgment totaled $5 million and no unconditional stay issued
sections.cue: Close this stage and identify later history without merging it into the ruling.
paragraphs: On February 4, 2008, Bennett retained liability, denied Rule 60 relief for lack of a specified basis, and granted reduction motions only as to punishment. The $2.9 million compensation plus $2.1 million punitive award totaled $5 million. Stays pending the posttrial motions became moot; a stay pending appeal awaited a bond or other security. The court granted no unconditional bond-free stay.

The original order confirms Fred’s $300,000 punitive allocation, despite a reproduction’s erroneous $800,000. The assignment reports later appellate reversal and Supreme Court affirmance of that appellate judgment. Those are distinct subsequent stages; this account explains the district court’s voir-dire and posttrial analysis rather than presenting its constitutional ruling as the final result.
